topic: How Do Satellites Stay in Space Without Falling Down?
angle: Thousands of heavy metal satellites hang hundreds of kilometers above the Earth in a permanent, infinite free-fall without ever crashing back to the ground.
why: Explainer videos breaking down complex orbital and physical mechanics consistently pull tens of millions of views because they challenge basic intuition. This question is irresistible because everyone looks up at the sky or uses GPS daily, yet the concept of 'falling sideways fast enough to miss the Earth' creates an immediate lightbulb moment.
keywords: how do satellites stay in orbit
why don't satellites fall to earth
how gravity and speed work in space
how do things stay in space
facts: Satellites in Low Earth Orbit fly at an incredible speed of about 28,000 kilometers per hour (17,500 miles per hour).
At this extreme speed, as gravity pulls the satellite down toward the Earth, the Earth's surface curves away at the exact same rate.
This continuous balancing act means the satellite is technically in a state of perpetual free-fall around the planet.
Because there is virtually no air resistance in the vacuum of space above 160 kilometers, the satellite does not slow down naturally.
If a satellite were to stop moving sideways instantly, gravity would pull it straight down into a fiery crash.
The higher a satellite is placed, the slower it needs to travel to maintain its orbit because Earth's gravitational pull weakens with distance.
Geostationary satellites orbit at about 35,786 kilometers above the equator, matching the exact rotational speed of the Earth.
This matching speed allows a geostationary satellite to hover constantly over the exact same spot on the ground for communications and weather tracking.
Even in Low Earth Orbit, tiny traces of Earth's upper atmosphere create microscopic drag, requiring satellites to carry small thrusters for periodic course corrections.
Without these occasional thruster burns, atmospheric drag would slowly decay their orbit and cause them to re-enter and burn up in the atmosphere within years.
